quotes.text: I wish you had the amount of living under your belt when you start writing songs. I write all the time, and I love what I'm writing so much more than I did when I was younger.

Partially because when you get older, you're liberated from worrying about whether it's going to be commercial, whether it's going to be a hit. There's something really deep about bearing witness. That's been a real gift for me, being my age and writing now.

You're right. You don't have the experience when you're young, but you certainly feel a lot of shit. My theory is that everybody experiences the same emotions. The stories are different, but it's always the same emotions. It's love, it's sadness, it's loss, it's joy. It's hope or anticipation. It's anger. It's resentment. It's all that, but it's the story that makes it really interesting.

Yeah, maybe more. There's a lot of stuff that goes into songwriting or goes into a song that a lot of people don't know. Sometimes people will sing at the top of their lungs and have absolutely no idea what they're singing about. "All I Wanna Do" was the most cynical song, but people love that chorus. So … sometimes the story matters less.
Yeah, yeah. It's about being disenfranchised, but it's fun to talk about that stuff. People want to know where a song was born, what it was born from. It makes it even more personal.
I don't generally say who things are about, mainly because it doesn't really matter. It's still the same experience.
In "My Favorite Mistake," that's always been the long-running joke. It's sort of like my version of Carly Simon's "You're So Vain." Was that Mick Jagger? Was it? Or was it Warren Beatty?
Yes, so I don't name names. To protect the … not so innocent.
I think there are a couple of people that assume it's about them. But it's only about one.
No. There's one person that knows. My manager. He's been with me since the beginning of time, so he pretty much knows where all the dead bodies are buried.

I just don't want it to be too literal, because I think it is a universal experience. Why put a face on it already? I can remember when videos started coming out, like VH1 and MTV, and as a songwriter, like, Oh, I hate that. Because it gives people a visual of what a song is that they attach to it.
Mine wouldn't diminish it. But I'm just saying—I'm not telling.

I'm starting off with "Run Baby Run," which actually was the very first single, and it was the very first song on my first record. That song we wrote the night that Bill Clinton was elected. I never sing it without thinking about the great hope that came with that. He was running against George Bush. He was like the MTV candidate. He was the first president that appealed to that generation.
Yes, he was so accessible and so galvanizing to the youth culture, and there was so much hope in that. So it's just interesting to sing that song.
Truth be told, [Be Myself] really is where I'm at. I feel like, 'Hey, I'm my age and I love it. And I don't want to be anybody else.' It's about acceptance.

I actually did go through a detox period. I keep my phone on me but it's always on silent. When I'm with my kids, I don't have my phone on me. I will never regret missing phone calls or texts or any of that to be present and to model that for my children. Because there will be a point in our evolution as people on this planet where it is going to cause some major problems.
